Title: Fake News: NASA Confirms 15 Days of Darkness?
In 2015 and later in 2017, an article under NASA was posted online, claiming that in November of that year, 15 days of darkness were inevitable.
They explained that this event hasn’t happened in a million years and was caused by an event happening to Venus and Jupiter.
It is important to note that the claim about NASA forecasting 15 days of darkness on Earth is a common example of an internet fake news tale.
The deceptive narrative stated that a time of utter darkness would occur in November, prompting readers to spread the news, be alarmed, and get confused.
However, this claim has no basis in reality and was debunked later on by NASA and various reputable sources.

A quick Google search and thorough research undertaken through credible sources and fact-checking organizations have disproved “15 Days of Darkness.” NASA, in particular, has denied the reality of such an event and stated that there is no scientific evidence to back up the story’s claims.
The story’s beginnings are unknown, but it is obvious that it spread mostly through social media platforms and online news agencies.
This study also emphasizes the ubiquity of fake news and the difficulties faced by the quick dissemination of disinformation in the digital world.
While there have been earlier stories and conspiracy theories about the Earth becoming black for a few days, such claims have continuously been shown to be erroneous and lacking any scientific basis.
One noteworthy example is the 2012 “end of the world” prediction associated with the Mayan calendar.
This forecast drew enormous attention and worry since it suggested that Earth will be destroyed by a cataclysmic event.
However, as we now understand, the Mayan calendar only represented the conclusion of a cycle, not the end of the planet.
Experts and scientists have categorically denied the “15 Days of Darkness” claim as a hoax.
NASA, the world’s premier space exploration agency, has said that no astronomical or scientific occurrence could generate such a lengthy stretch of darkness on Earth.

The article attemps to use this evidence as stated in the article “_The stories also falsely attribute the science behind the blackout to_ _Charles Bolden_ _, the former head of NASA under the Obama administration.

The stories claim that Bolden wrote “a detailed 1000 pages document … explaining the strange event to officials at the White House.” There is no evidence of such a document, and Bolden’s work has_ _focused_ _on developing missions into space, not the physical science of astronomical phenomena_”.Astronomical organizations and other reliable sources have also supplied answers that refute the story’s incorrect claims.
Their professional judgments, backed up by scientific facts, provide persuasive arguments against the story’s veracity.
The “15 Days of Darkness” false news tale serves as a reminder of the value of media literacy and critical thinking in the face of exaggerated claims.
Through thorough research and professional analysis, it is clear that the narrative has no basis in scientific truth.
The quick spread of such false information emphasizes the importance of informed information consumption and fact-checking.
We can navigate the digital realm more efficiently and shield ourselves from the influence of false news by remaining watchful and relying on reputable sources.
